what: InterDigital owns patents and licenses them. Its portfolio covers wireless standards such as 4G, 5G and Wi-Fi, and video compression standards used in streaming and displays. It does not make products; it collects royalties from companies that do.
customers: Smartphone makers, television and display manufacturers, streaming video services and consumer electronics companies. Agreements are negotiated company by company and often follow litigation.
money: Royalties from handset makers using cellular and Wi-Fi standards.
Televisions, tablets, computers and connected devices.
Licences covering video compression used by streaming platforms.
moat: Its patents are declared essential to standards that the whole industry must implement, so anyone building a 5G phone or a modern television needs a licence. The company employs engineers who contribute to standards bodies, which keeps the portfolio relevant as standards evolve.
risks: Revenue is lumpy. It depends on when agreements are signed, so $868.5M in 2024 fell to $834.0M in 2025 and periods without a major renewal look weak.
Growth depends on litigation outcomes. A court ruling that royalty rates are too high would reset the economics across many agreements.
A handful of large licensees account for much of the revenue, so one renegotiation matters enormously.
The shares trade at about 30 times earnings, which assumes further successful licence expansion.
Only three analysts cover the stock, and the $462.67 average target against a $270.75 price is an extremely wide gap on minimal coverage.
opportunities: Net margin is very high at roughly 49%, because collecting royalties costs little once a licence exists.
Cash of about $1.2B exceeds debt of $492.3M, and free cash flow of $252.0M funds dividends and buybacks.
Each new licence signed with a previously unlicensed manufacturer adds almost pure profit.
Video and streaming licensing is the newest area and still has many unlicensed potential payers.
watch: New licence agreements signed. Revenue in this business arrives in steps rather than a smooth line, so the announcement of a major agreement, not quarterly revenue, is what changes the value.
